case_title: S. K. Miglani v. State NCT of Delhi
accused_occupation: Bank manager (Manager, Bank of Baroda, Faridabad Branch)
statutory_provisions: Charged: IPC s.465, s.120-B. FIR/charge sheet also listed IPC ss.201, 409, 419, 420, 467, 468, 471, 120-B
evidence_type: Documentary evidence; forensic handwriting/signature expert opinion
trial_court_outcome: Discharge application rejected for want of s.197 Cr.P.C. sanction (order of 03.12.2014); charges framed under IPC ss.465 and 120-B on 13.12.2014. No verdict or sentence.
high_court_outcome: Section 482 Cr.P.C. petition dismissed; CMM orders upheld (judgment dated 06.08.2018)
neutral_facts: A written complaint by a housing development director in November 2000 led to an FIR alleging a fraud on a housing authority concerning a flat allotted to the victim. The prosecution case was that several housing authority employees, together with property dealers and a special power of attorney holder, acted on a request purportedly made by the allottee to reduce the flat's cost, and that the original fixed deposit receipt and refund application were found removed or misplaced from the file. The FIR further alleged that a refund cheque of Rs.2,22,263 was withdrawn through a savings bank account opened at a bank branch with a forged signature of the allottee. The investigation later alleged that the accused, then a branch manager at that bank, opened a savings account in the allottee's name in connivance with others, in order to encash the cheque dated 7 January 2000. The prosecution relied on a forensic handwriting report dated 30 December 2002 comparing the signature on the account opening form with the accused's specimen signatures. That report stated that a definite opinion could not be given on the remaining items on the materials available. A further report was later sought from a government examiner of questioned documents, which, according to the submissions recorded, expressed an opinion that the signature on the account opening form tallied with the accused's specimen signatures.
financial_property_loss: Refund cheque of Rs.2,22,263 (alleged to have been withdrawn through forged account)
premeditation_planning: Not stated; conspiracy is alleged in the charge but the court made no finding on it
motive: alleged: to encash the refund cheque through a fictitious savings account
key_evidence_accepted: None accepted on merits; the court held the FSL handwriting report's evidentiary value is to be assessed at trial
trial_duration: offence: 1996 and afterwards (as alleged in charge); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 06.08.2018; Supreme Court: 30.04.2019
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Ajayinder Sangwan, Rajkumar Sharma, V.P. Singh, T.P. Singh and others (Advs.); State NCT of Delhi: V. Balaji, Nachiketa Joshi, Praneet Pranav, B.V. Balaram Das (Advs.)
investigation_status: FIR No. 432 of 2000 registered 15.11.2000; charge sheet and supplementary charge sheet filed naming the accused; FSL reports obtained; charge framed 13.12.2014
procedural_irregularity: Magistrate's order at the discharge stage recorded a conclusive opinion that the accused committed forgery, which the court held should have been avoided
appeal_history: Trial court (CMM): discharge rejected 03.12.2014, charges framed 13.12.2014. High Court: s.482 petition dismissed 06.08.2018. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; s.197 rejection upheld, forgery observations deleted
prosecution_argument: Section 197 does not apply because forgery and related offences cannot be committed in discharge of official duty (relying on Parkash Singh Badal); the CMM rightly rejected discharge
defence_argument: Accused was a public servant and sanction under s.197 was required; account was opened in discharge of official duty; the later handwriting report is unreliable and handwriting opinion is weak evidence; CMM wrongly held forgery proved before trial
legal_principle_applied: Section 197 applies only to a public servant not removable from office save by or with the sanction of the Government; if not met, the official-duty question need not be examined. Magistrate must avoid conclusive opinion on investigation evidence before final trial
precedent_relied_upon: K.Ch. Prasad v. J. Vanalatha Devi (1987) 2 SCC 52 (relied on); Parkash Singh Badal v. State of Punjab (2007) 1 SCC 1; Inspector of Police v. Battenapatla Venkata Ratnam (2015) 13 SCC 87; Devinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2016) 12 SCC 87; N.K. Ganguly v. CBI (2016) 2 SCC 143; S.P.S. Rathore v. CBI (2017) 5 SCC 817 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: Observations in the CMM order of 03.12.2014 that the accused forged the signatures and that an act of forgery by a public servant is not official duty are deleted; no other order
